facts.claim: Bowlby's Maternal Care and Mental Health was published by the World Health Organization in 1951.
facts.mechanism: Because The WHO commission synthesized evidence about institutional care and prolonged separation to inform child welfare practice.
facts.commonError: Attachment theory began as Harlow's interpretation of monkey experiments.
facts.whyWrong: Bowlby's human clinical and institutional work developed in parallel and supplied the evolutionary framework.

facts.claim: Bowlby treated attachment behavior as an evolved system for maintaining protective proximity to a caregiver.
facts.mechanism: Because Infants who restore closeness under danger gain protection before they can survive independently.
facts.commonError: Crying and clinging are learned only because a caregiver supplies food.
facts.whyWrong: Attachment behaviors organize safety and proximity beyond feeding episodes.

facts.claim: Harlow's original surrogate-mother study used eight newborn rhesus monkeys divided across two feeding arrangements.
facts.mechanism: Because Reversing whether cloth or wire supplied milk separated contact comfort from nourishment.
facts.commonError: Every monkey received milk only from the wire surrogate.
facts.whyWrong: Milk location was counterbalanced across two groups of four.

facts.claim: Infant rhesus monkeys strongly preferred the cloth surrogate even when the wire surrogate supplied milk.
facts.mechanism: Because Soft contact and a usable haven under threat had value independent of caloric reinforcement.
facts.commonError: The monkeys preferred whichever surrogate fed them.
facts.whyWrong: Time spent clinging followed cloth covering more than milk location.

facts.claim: Attachment bonds are identified by proximity maintenance, separation distress, safe haven, and secure base.
facts.mechanism: Because Together the four functions describe staying near, reacting to loss, seeking comfort, and exploring from safety.
facts.commonError: Attachment is measured only by how upset someone becomes during separation.
facts.whyWrong: Separation distress is one of four defining functions.

facts.claim: Hazan and Shaver applied attachment theory to adult romantic love in a 1987 study.
facts.mechanism: Because Adult partners can provide proximity, comfort, and security functions analogous to those in earlier bonds.
facts.commonError: Attachment theory concerns only infants and parents.
facts.whyWrong: The adult extension generated a large research program on romantic attachment.

facts.claim: The early Hazan-Shaver study recruited respondents through the Rocky Mountain News.
facts.mechanism: Because A newspaper questionnaire allowed adult readers to classify relationship experience and report romantic histories at scale.
facts.commonError: The original adult-attachment evidence came from observed couples in a clinical laboratory.
facts.whyWrong: The landmark first study relied substantially on self-report from newspaper respondents.

facts.claim: Peer relationships acquire attachment functions gradually across childhood and adolescence.
facts.mechanism: Because Preferences for proximity, comfort, and exploration shift at different rates rather than transferring all at once.
facts.commonError: A first romance instantly replaces parents in every attachment role.
facts.whyWrong: The four functions show a staged transfer across age and relationship development.

facts.claim: Passionate love and companionate love have different typical dynamics.
facts.mechanism: Because Novelty, longing, and arousal can intensify rapidly, while trust, shared history, and caregiving accumulate through repeated interaction.
facts.commonError: A decline in early intensity proves that love has ended.
facts.whyWrong: A bond can shift toward companionate attachment even as acute passion becomes less constant.
